title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
Preface
A practical guide to getting work done on MedicineBow, the University of Wyoming’s high-performance computing (HPC) cluster, run by the Advanced Research Computing Center (ARCC).
It is written for people joining the ASCEND engine and its ARID program, and assumes you are comfortable on a computer but have never used a shared supercomputer. Each chapter explains why before how.

title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
Why this book exists
The official documentation — the ARCC wiki — is good but has gaps and is in places out of date. The content here was written while onboarding on the live cluster and cross-checked against the running system in July 2026. Where the docs and the machine disagree, this book follows the machine and notes the conflict.






This is not an official ARCC document



It’s a community onboarding guide. It can drift out of date, and ARCC can change policy at any time. When in doubt, the official wiki and arcc-help@uwyo.edu are authoritative. Corrections are very welcome.

title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
Quick orientation

You cannot request your own account — your PI must. No project, no account. (See 2  Getting an account.)
Nothing on the cluster is backed up. Not home, not project, not scratch. There are snapshots, but they live on the same array. (See 5  Where your data lives.)
Never run real computation on a login node. Log in, then hand work to the scheduler (Slurm) or grab an interactive session. (See 9  Why a scheduler exists.)
Every job must name your project account with --account=<project>. (See 10  Anatomy of a batch job.)
The partition and QOS you choose decide how long you wait and how big you can go. Short test runs and long simulations belong in different queues (12  Partitions and QOS on MedicineBow, 13  Queue times: which partition for what).

title: Getting Started on ARCC MedicineBow
text:
How the book is organized

Part I .
Part II is a minimal Linux survival kit.
Part III covers the filesystems and moving data in and out.
Part IV covers software: modules, conda, and containers.
Part V covers Slurm, the batch scheduler — how to ask for resources, pick a queue, watch your jobs, run arrays, use GPUs, and handle preemption and failures.
Part VI is quick reference: a cheat sheet, troubleshooting, and a glossary.

Conventions: shell commands you type are shown in code blocks. Boxes marked Gotcha or Important mark places people reliably get burned.

title: 1  What a cluster is
text:
1.1 Mental model
MedicineBow is not one big computer. It is a few hundred ordinary Linux servers (“nodes”) wired together, all mounting the same shared filesystems, all managed by a program that decides whose job runs where and when. That program is the scheduler (here, Slurm). Learning the cluster is mostly learning to work with the scheduler.

title: 1  What a cluster is
text:
1.2 Login nodes vs. compute nodes
There are two kinds of machines, and confusing them is the most common beginner mistake.
Login nodes (mblog1, mblog2) are the front door. When you ssh in or open a terminal in the web portal, you land here. They are shared by everyone at once — dozens of people editing files, submitting jobs, and moving data. Use them for lightweight work: editing scripts, managing files, compiling small things, submitting and checking jobs.
Compute nodes are where computation happens. You never SSH to them directly; you ask the scheduler for one (or many), and it gives you exclusive, accounted-for access for a bounded time. The default mb nodes have 96 CPU cores and ~1 TB of RAM each, and the GPU nodes carry up to 8 NVIDIA H100s.

Figure 1.1: You reach a shared login node from your laptop; the scheduler runs your jobs on dedicated compute nodes. All nodes see the same filesystems.











Don’t compute on login nodes



A heavy job on mblog1/mblog2 — a big simulation, a data-crunching Python script, a multi-hour build — slows the machine for everyone logging in. ARCC monitors this and kills runaway login-node processes (and emails you).
Rule of thumb: anything that takes more than a couple of minutes, or uses more than a core or two, belongs in a Slurm job or an interactive session. See Chapter 9.

title: 1  What a cluster is
section: 1.3 Why share a machine at all?
text:
1.3 Why share a machine at all?
If everyone had their own dedicated server, most servers would sit idle while a few people occasionally needed far more than one server could give. Pooling the hardware and scheduling access means:

When you need 50 nodes for an ensemble, you can have them (briefly).
When you need nothing, someone else uses the hardware you’re not using.
A fair-share accounting system stops any one person from hogging everything.

In exchange, you sometimes wait in line and you have to describe your work up front (how many cores, how much memory, how long). Most of this book is about making those two things painless.

title: 1  What a cluster is
text:
1.4 What MedicineBow is, concretely
MedicineBow is a RHEL 9 Linux cluster. Its hardware is a mix of:

General CPU nodes (the mb partition): 25 nodes, 96 cores and ~1 TB RAM each.
GPU nodes: H100, L40S, A30, A6000, and R6000 flavors — for ML, PINNs, and anything CUDA.
Absorbed older clusters: the retired Teton, Beartooth, and WildIris clusters now live on as large partitions inside MedicineBow. Teton alone is ~250 nodes.
Investor (“condo”) nodes: hardware bought by specific research groups, which others can borrow when it’s idle — but the owner can reclaim it and bump your job (see Chapter 18).

You don’t need to memorize this. The partition chapter (Chapter 12) covers which hardware to ask for, and the queue-times chapter (Chapter 13) covers which choices leave you waiting versus running now.

2.1 How accounts work
ARCC will not create an account without written confirmation from a Principal Investigator who owns a project. Accounts are tied to funded projects for accounting and fair-share purposes.
So the first step is a conversation, not a form:
For ASCEND/ARID performers the project is something like cowy-firesurro (the project this guide was written under). Confirm the exact project name with your PI — you type it into every job you run (Chapter 10).

title: 2  Getting an account
text:
2.4 The free tier
Each researcher’s baseline allocation:

100,000 CPU core-hours per year
20,000 GPU-hours per year

That is plenty for getting started — 100,000 core-hours is roughly one 96-core node running flat out for six weeks. Larger allocations and investor projects exist beyond this. Core-hours are counted as (cores × wall-clock hours), a reason not to over-ask for resources (Chapter 11).

title: 2  Getting an account
text:
2.5 The practical checklist

Confirm with your PI which project you’re joining and its exact name.
Have the PI email arcc-help@uwyo.edu to request your account on that project. (You emailing them yourself won’t work — they need the PI’s confirmation.)
Once ARCC provisions you, you’ll get a UW username. Your first login is Chapter 3.
If you’re an external collaborator, flag it now and ask how you’ll move data, since Globus won’t be available to you.

No VPN is required to reach ARCC, on campus or off, so once your account exists you can log in from anywhere.

title: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys
text:
The web portal (Open OnDemand) is a browser interface: a file explorer, a terminal, job submission forms, and interactive apps (desktop sessions, RStudio, Jupyter). Start here on day one.
SSH is the terminal way in, and how you’ll work day-to-day once set up. It requires a key you generate through the portal first.







Don’t use “Southpass”



Older notes may point you at southpass.arcc.uwyo.edu, the portal for the retired Beartooth cluster. The DNS name still resolves but has no live service behind it. The current portal is medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu.

title: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys
text:
3.2 Step 1 — Log into the portal
Go to https://medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu and sign in with your UW username and password. You’ll be prompted for Duo two-factor authentication. If you’ve never set up Duo, do it at https://wyosecure.uwyo.edu. No VPN is needed.
Once in, note the Files menu (browse /home, /project, /gscratch), the Clusters → Shell option (a terminal in your browser), and the Interactive Apps menu.

title: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys
section: 3.3 Step 2 — Generate your SSH key with the SSH Key Manager
text:
3.3 Step 2 — Generate your SSH key with the SSH Key Manager
SSH on MedicineBow is key-and-certificate based, not password based. Generate a key pair through the portal:

In the portal, open the SSH Key Manager.
Generate a key. It downloads as a zip named after your username.
Unpack it into your local ~/.ssh and fix permissions:

unzip ~/Downloads/<username>.zip -d ~/.ssh
chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh
ssh-add
Now you can connect from your own terminal:
ssh <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu






SSH keys expire after one year



Roughly a year after setup, your ssh stops working — permission denied, no obvious reason. The key expired. Go back to the portal’s SSH Key Manager, generate a fresh key, and unzip it into ~/.ssh again. This is by design.
crumbs: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys

title: 3  First login, the portal, and SSH keys
text:
3.4 Step 3 — A comfortable SSH config (optional)
Add this to ~/.ssh/config on your laptop so you can just type ssh medbow:
Host medbow
    HostName medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu
    User <username>
    ServerAliveInterval 60
    ServerAliveCountMax 5
ServerAliveInterval sends a small keepalive every 60 seconds so campus/VPN firewalls don’t silently drop your connection while you’re reading output.

title: 4  Linux essentials
text:
4.1 Moving around
If you already live in a terminal, skim the tmux section. Everything here is standard Linux; nothing is ARCC-specific except the paths.
Three shortcuts you’ll use constantly: ~ is your home directory, . is “here”, and .. is “up one”. Press Tab to complete a half-typed path.

title: 4  Linux essentials
text:
pwd                 # where am I?
ls -lh              # list files, human-readable sizes
cd /project/cowy-firesurro   # go somewhere
cd                  # go home ($HOME)
cd -                # go back to where you just were

title: 4  Linux essentials
section: 4.2 Looking at files without opening them
text:
4.2 Looking at files without opening them
cat file.txt          # dump a whole (small) file
less big.log          # page through a big file; q to quit, / to search
head -n 20 file       # first 20 lines
tail -n 50 file       # last 50 lines
tail -f slurm-123.out # follow a job's output live as it's written
tail -f on a job’s output file shows whether it’s doing anything.

title: 4  Linux essentials
text:
4.3 Editing files
nano is the easy choice — arrow keys work, and shortcuts are listed at the bottom of the screen (^O = save, ^X = exit).
nano submit.sh
vim is powerful but has a learning curve; if you don’t know it, nano is fine for a submit script. For anything bigger, edit on your laptop and use the portal’s file browser, VS Code’s Remote-SSH, or rsync (Chapter 6).

title: 4  Linux essentials
text:
4.4 Finding things
grep -r "account" .          # search file contents recursively
find . -name "*.nc"          # find files by name
find . -size +1G             # find files bigger than 1 GB (great for quota hunts)
du -sh *                     # how big is each thing in this directory?
du -sh * | sort -h finds what’s eating your quota — useful given the 50 GB home limit (Chapter 5).

title: 4  Linux essentials
text:
4.5 Environment variables and your shell
Your shell remembers settings in variables. A few you’ll meet:
echo $HOME        # /home/<username>
echo $USER        # your username
echo $SCRATCH     # /gscratch/<username> — your scratch space
echo $PATH        # where the shell looks for commands
To make something permanent (say, a handy alias), add it to ~/.bashrc:
alias q='squeue --me'          # see just my jobs
alias proj='cd /project/cowy-firesurro'
Run source ~/.bashrc (or log out and back in) to apply changes.

title: 4  Linux essentials
section: 4.6 tmux: keep work alive across a dropped connection
text:
4.6 tmux: keep work alive across a dropped connection
When you SSH in and start something, closing your laptop or losing WiFi kills that shell and everything running in it. tmux keeps your session alive on the login node whether or not you’re connected.
tmux new -s work     # start a named session "work"
#   ... do things, launch an interactive job, watch output ...
#   detach with:  Ctrl-b then d
tmux ls              # list your sessions
tmux attach -t work  # reattach later, even from a different computer
The workflow:

SSH into the login node.
tmux new -s work.
Inside tmux, do your editing, submit jobs, launch an interactive session (Chapter 17).
Detach (Ctrl-b then d) and close your laptop. It all keeps running.
Tomorrow, SSH back in and tmux attach -t work — exactly where you left off.







tmux is for login-node shells, not batch jobs



A batch job (sbatch, Chapter 10) already runs independently of your connection — log out and it keeps going. tmux is for things that live in your shell: interactive sessions, monitoring, an editor you don’t want to lose.

title: 4  Linux essentials
text:
4.7 Permissions, briefly
You’ll occasionally see chmod and permission strings like -rw-r-----. The main uses are fixing your SSH keys (chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh, from Chapter 3) and making a script executable:
chmod +x run.sh
There is no sudo on the cluster. You can’t install system packages or change things outside your own directories, and you don’t need to — everything you install goes in your own space (Chapter 8) or as modules (Chapter 7).

title: 5  Where your data lives
text:
5.1 Nothing is backed up
Nothing on MedicineBow is backed up. Not home, not project, not scratch.
There are snapshots (point-in-time copies you can sometimes restore from), but they live on the same storage array as your live data — if the array fails, the snapshots fail with it. Snapshots protect against accidental deletion, not hardware loss. Anything you can’t afford to lose needs a copy elsewhere: your institution’s storage, a cloud bucket, or the separate Alcova service, which does have real nightly backups.

Check your usage and limits for home, scratch, and project:
arccquota

5.2.1 /home — small, personal, for config not data
50 GB fills fast once a conda environment eats 15 GB of it. Home is for dotfiles, scripts, and small configs — not datasets and not software installs. When home fills up, things break (jobs fail to write logs, logins misbehave), so watch it with arccquota and du -sh ~/* | sort -h.


5.2.2 /project/<proj> — the shared workhorse
5 TB, shared by everyone on your project (e.g. cowy-firesurro). This is where shared datasets, inputs, and results belong. Agree on a directory convention with your group so you don’t clobber each other. It persists for 6 months after the project ends.


5.2.3 /gscratch/$USER — fast and disposable
Also 5 TB, and the fast filesystem — use it as the working directory for jobs with heavy I/O. Files untouched for 90 days are purged automatically. Never keep the only copy of anything here.






Scratch purge is 90 days, not 45



Legacy Confluence docs say 45 days; the current ARCC wiki says 90. Both pages are live, but 90 is the current policy. Either way, don’t treat scratch as storage.




5.2.4 /lscratch — node-local, gone when the job ends
Each compute node has its own local disk at /lscratch. It’s the fastest storage available to a job (no network in the way), ideal for scratch files a single job reads and rewrites constantly. It’s wiped when your job ends, so copy anything you want to keep back to /project or /gscratch before the job exits.
(There is no /data filesystem, despite what some docs suggest.)

5.3 Install software in project space, not home

title: 6  Moving data in and out
section: 6.2 Globus — the recommended path for real data
text:
6.2 Globus — the recommended path for real data
Globus transfers between “collections” (endpoints). It’s restartable, checksums what it moves, retries failures, and runs server-side, so you can start a multi-hundred-GB transfer, close your laptop, and get an email when it’s done.

Log in at https://app.globus.org (choose “University of Wyoming” as your organization, or your own institution).
Search collections for uwyo-ARCC and pick “Medicine Bow”.
The Medicine Bow collection’s root is cluster, so your project shows up at a path like /cluster/medbow/project/cowy-firesurro/....
Set the other side to your institutional or personal collection (install Globus Connect Personal on your own machine to make it an endpoint), pick files, and hit Start.







Globus needs a full UW account



ARCC-Only accounts (external collaborators — Chapter 2) cannot use Globus. If your data lives at CSU, CU, or NCAR and you’re on an ARCC-Only account, you’ll need a UW-side person to broker the transfer, or a guest collection set up for you.

6  Moving data in and out

title: 6  Moving data in and out
section: 6.3 scp and rsync — fine for small, everyday transfers
text:
6.3 scp and rsync — fine for small, everyday transfers
From your laptop, push a file up:
scp results.csv <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/project/cowy-firesurro/<you>/
Pull one down:
scp <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/gscratch/<you>/output.nc .
rsync is better for directories and for resuming — it only copies what changed, so an interrupted transfer picks up where it left off:
rsync -avP ./localdir/ <username>@medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu:/project/cowy-firesurro/<you>/dir/
The -P flag shows progress and enables resume; -a preserves timestamps and permissions. For more than a few GB, prefer Globus — a login-node scp of a huge file competes with everyone else’s login-node activity and will be slow.

title: 6  Moving data in and out
section: 6.4 rclone — cloud storage (S3, Google Drive, Box…)
text:
6.4 rclone — cloud storage (S3, Google Drive, Box…)
rclone is ARCC’s recommended CLI for moving data to and from cloud services. It’s a module:
module load rclone/1.63.1
rclone config          # one-time: set up a "remote" (S3 bucket, Drive, etc.)
rclone copy mydata/ myremote:bucket/path/    # copy up
rclone copy myremote:bucket/path/ ./mydata/  # copy down
rclone verifies and retries, and handles many small files far better than a loop of scps.

title: 7  Software modules
text:
7.1 Why modules exist
A cluster has hundreds of users who need incompatible software: three versions of Python, five compilers, conflicting builds of GDAL. Modules let you load exactly the versions you want into your shell for this session, without affecting anyone else. Load a module and its programs appear on your PATH; unload it and they vanish.

title: 7  Software modules
text:
module load gcc/14.2.0        # add gcc 14 to this shell
module list                   # what do I currently have loaded?
module unload gcc/14.2.0      # remove it
module purge                  # clear everything and start clean

title: 7  Software modules
text:
7.2 The hierarchy
MedicineBow uses Lmod in hierarchical mode. Modules are arranged in layers:

Core modules are always visible: the compilers (gcc, nvhpc-sdk, oneapi), MPI, and standalone tools.
Compiler-dependent modules — Python, R, GDAL, NetCDF, HDF5, CUDA — are hidden until you load a compiler. They were built against a specific compiler, so Lmod won’t show them until you’ve picked one.

So a new user runs module avail, doesn’t see gdal, and concludes it isn’t installed. It is — just one layer down.






Use module spider, not module avail, to check whether something exists



module avail shows only what’s loadable given what you’ve already loaded. module spider searches the entire tree and tells you both that something exists and what to load first to reach it.
module spider gdal            # yes it exists; here are the versions
module spider gdal/3.13.0     # ...and exactly what to load before it


A typical geospatial stack, in order:
module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0        # 1. a compiler, first
module load gdal/3.13.0       # 2. now GDAL is reachable
module load netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi

title: 7  Software modules
text:
7.3 What’s installed (a tour)
Ask the machine for the current list with module spider, but roughly:

Compilers (core): gcc/{11.4.0, 11.5.0, 13.2.0, 14.2.0, 15.2.0}, nvhpc-sdk, oneapi, openmpi/5.0.10.
After loading a compiler: python/{3.10.6, 3.12.0, 3.14.4}, r/{4.4.0, 4.5.3}, gdal/{3.7.3, 3.13.0}, netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi, hdf5/1.14.3*, cuda-toolkit/{12.4.1, 12.6.1}, openmpi/4.1.6, rclone/1.63.1.
Standalone: apptainer/{1.3.5, 1.4.1}, singularity/4.1.0, miniconda3/24.3.0, julia/{1.10.3, 1.11.6}.







CUDA needs the deprecated gcc/13.2.0



gcc/13.2.0 prints a deprecation warning pointing to gcc/14.2.0, but cuda-toolkit is only built against gcc/13.2.0. GPU users have to load it anyway:
module load gcc/13.2.0        # the one that warns you — CUDA needs it
module load cuda-toolkit/12.6.1
Ignore the warning here; it’s a packaging quirk.

title: 7  Software modules
section: 7.4 Making a set of modules load automatically
text:
7.4 Making a set of modules load automatically
Once you know the stack a project needs, save it as a named collection so you don’t retype it:
module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 gdal/3.13.0 netcdf-c/4.9.2-ompi
module save geostack          # remember this set as "geostack"

# next session:
module restore geostack
Prefer module restore in submit scripts over hand-loading a long list — it’s reproducible and self-documents the environment your job needs.






Load modules in your submit script, not just interactively



Modules loaded on the login node don’t carry into a batch job. Put the module load / module restore lines inside your sbatch script so the job builds the same environment every time (Chapter 10).


When a package isn’t available as a module — or you need a pip/conda world — see the next chapter (Chapter 8).

text:
8.1 Point conda away from home first
The miniconda3 module gives you conda:
By default, conda writes environments and a package cache into ~/.conda and ~/miniconda3, inside your 50 GB home quota. A couple of scientific environments will fill it. Before creating any environments, point conda at your project’s 250 GB software space.
Create ~/.condarc:
Now new environments and the download cache land in project space:

section: 8.2 Apptainer: containers for reproducibility and portability
text:
8.2 Apptainer: containers for reproducibility and portability
A container bundles an application with its entire operating-system environment into a single image file. On HPC the runtime is Apptainer (formerly Singularity). It runs containers as you, with no root, which makes it the HPC-safe alternative to Docker.
module load apptainer/1.4.1

# Pull a Docker image and convert it to an Apptainer image (.sif):
apptainer pull mytool.sif docker://ghcr.io/someorg/mytool:latest

# Run something inside it:
apptainer exec mytool.sif mytool --help

# Bind your data into the container so it can see it:
apptainer exec --bind /project/cowy-firesurro:/data mytool.sif mytool /data/input.nc
Store .sif images in /project/<proj>/software — they can be large.

GPUs inside containers



To use the node’s GPUs from inside a container, add the --nv flag so Apptainer exposes the NVIDIA driver: apptainer exec --nv mytool.sif .... Pair this with a GPU job (Section 17.2).


Next: running your work through the scheduler (Part V, starting at Chapter 9).

title: 9  Why a scheduler exists
text:
9.1 Why share a machine
With 300 researchers, 300 nodes, and no scheduler, everyone logs into whatever node looks idle and starts running. Two jobs land on the same node and thrash its memory until both crash. A two-week run occupies the node you need for a five-minute test. Nobody can tell whether a node is free.
Slurm replaces “grab a node and hope” with a contract:
The rest of this book is about writing that description well.

title: 9  Why a scheduler exists
text:
You describe the work: resources and a time limit.
Slurm reserves exactly that, on nodes that can provide it, and accounts for it.
Your job runs with those resources guaranteed and isolated from other jobs.
When your time limit is up, the job ends, which keeps the line moving.

title: 9  Why a scheduler exists
section: 9.2 The two ways to run work
text:
9.2 The two ways to run work
Batch jobs (sbatch) are the normal mode: you write a script that lists the resources you need and the commands to run, submit it, and walk away. Slurm runs it when your turn comes and writes the output to a file. Use this for essentially all real computation. (Chapter 10)
Interactive jobs (salloc) give you a live shell on a compute node for debugging, exploring data, or developing a script. You still go through the scheduler and consume your allocation, but you get a prompt instead of a script. (Chapter 17)
Both run on compute nodes, not the login node (Chapter 1).

10.6 Useful variables inside a job
Slurm sets environment variables your script can use:

title: 11  Asking for resources
text:
11.1 Cores, tasks, and the words Slurm uses
For most jobs you need two ideas:
Asking for 8 cores does not make a single-threaded program faster; it reserves 7 idle cores and makes you wait longer. Match the request to what your code can use.

title: 11  Asking for resources
text:
A task is one instance of your program. Most jobs are a single task.
CPUs per task is how many cores that program can use (its threads).

#SBATCH --nodes=1                # keep a job on one node unless it's true MPI
#SBATCH --ntasks=1               # one program instance
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8        # that can use 8 cores

Single-threaded program? --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=1.
Multithreaded (OpenMP, most numpy/xarray work)? --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=N, and set export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK.
MPI across many nodes? Use --nodes and --ntasks, and launch with srun (Chapter 20).

title: 11  Asking for resources
text:
11.2 Memory
Set memory explicitly, every time. Two ways:
#SBATCH --mem=32G              # total memory for the whole job (simplest)
# or
#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G       # memory per core (scales with --cpus-per-task)






The 10 GB/core default on mb



If you omit --mem on the default partition, you get 10 GB per core, so --cpus-per-task=8 becomes an 80 GB request. That queues slower and can be rejected if it exceeds a limit. Set your memory explicitly. (Full story in Chapter 10.)


For a first run, estimate a bit high so the job isn’t killed, then measure and right-size (below). A job that exceeds its memory request is killed by the out-of-memory (OOM) killer (Chapter 19), so memory is the one resource where running out is fatal rather than slow.

title: 11  Asking for resources
text:
11.3 Time
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00        # HH:MM:SS  (or D-HH:MM:SS, e.g. 2-00:00:00)
Your job is killed the instant it hits this limit, so the request must exceed the real runtime; pad by roughly 25%. Don’t pad wildly, though: a shorter time limit means a lower QOS ceiling and better odds of backfilling into gaps, so it often starts sooner (Chapter 13).






No per-partition default time, so set --time



Partitions on MedicineBow don’t set a default wall time. Without --time, you inherit the partition maximum (7 days), which your QOS will likely reject (the normal QOS caps at 3 days). Always set --time yourself.

title: 11  Asking for resources
text:
11.4 Over-asking slows you down
A bigger request is a rarer set of free resources to find:

More cores / memory → fewer nodes can satisfy you → longer wait, and you’re charged for cores you didn’t use.
More time → lower-priority QOS tier and fewer backfill opportunities → longer wait.
A GPU you don’t use → you sit in the busy GPU queue for nothing (Chapter 13).

The fix is to right-size.

title: 11  Asking for resources
text:
11.5 Measure, then right-size, with seff
After a job finishes, seff tells you what it actually used versus what you reserved:
seff 123456
Job ID: 123456
State: COMPLETED
Cores: 8
CPU Efficiency: 24.13% of 04:16:00 core-walltime      <- you used ~2 of 8 cores
Memory Utilized: 5.31 GB
Memory Efficiency: 16.59% of 32.00 GB                 <- 32G reserved, 5G used
Read that as: next time ask for ~2 cores and ~8 GB. Low CPU efficiency means you reserved cores your code can’t use; low memory efficiency means you can ask for far less and start sooner.
Check what you’re allowed to ask for with ARCC’s helper:
showuserlimits
Next: where to send the job — partitions and QOS, and their queue-time consequences (Chapter 12, Chapter 13).

title: 12  Partitions and QOS on MedicineBow
text:
12.1 Partition = which hardware
A partition is a named pool of nodes. Submit with --partition=<name> (the default is mb).
¹ One L40S node has 4 GPUs instead of 8. Numbers are the machine as observed in July 2026; verify current state with showpartitions and sinfo.
Teton, Beartooth, and WildIris are retired clusters now folded into MedicineBow as large partitions; Teton alone is ~250 nodes. The inv-* partitions are investor (“condo”) hardware: you can run on them when they’re idle, but the owner can reclaim the node and preempt your job (Chapter 18).
You can list several partitions and let Slurm use whichever frees up first; --partition=mb,teton,beartooth is common for CPU throughput work.

title: 14  How priority is computed
text:
14.1 The formula
Slurm computes a priority score for every pending job and runs the highest scores first (subject to backfill, below). The score is a weighted sum; MedicineBow’s weights are:
Each factor is a number between 0 and 1, multiplied by its weight, and summed. The biggest lever, by a wide margin, is QOS.

title: 14  How priority is computed
text:
PriorityWeightQOS       = 200     <- dominant
PriorityWeightFairShare = 100
PriorityWeightJobSize   = 100
PriorityWeightAge       = 10
PriorityWeightPartition = 0       (partition doesn't affect priority here)

title: 14  How priority is computed
text:
14.2 What each factor means
QOS (weight 200). Higher-priority QOS means a better position. From Chapter 12: interactive (90) > fast (80) > normal (70) > long (60). Choosing fast over long is worth more priority than any amount of waiting, which is why the short-vs-long decision in Chapter 13 matters.
Fair-share (weight 100) — recent usage. Slurm tracks how much your account has used lately relative to its share. Heavy use this week lowers your fair-share factor, and thus your priority, for a while; it recovers as usage decays (half-life ~7 days here). This mechanism stops any one group from monopolizing the machine and rewards steady use over bursts.
Job size (weight 100). A factor based on the resources requested. With the SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME flag this cluster sets, it interacts with your time request — another reason not to over-ask (Chapter 11).
Age (weight 10) — time spent waiting. A job gains priority the longer it sits, maxing out after ~3 days. At weight 10, age is a tie-breaker, not a strategy; you won’t age past someone who chose a better QOS.

title: 14  How priority is computed
text:
14.3 Practical takeaway






QOS dominates priority



Because QOS is weighted 2× fair-share and 20× age, the highest-leverage choice for start time is the most appropriate high-priority QOS your job fits — the shortest walltime tier that still lets it finish (Chapter 13). Waiting longer, resubmitting, or submitting at 3am have little effect by comparison.

title: 14  How priority is computed
section: 14.4 Backfill: why a small job can jump the line
text:
14.4 Backfill: why a small job can jump the line
Priority sets the order, but Slurm also backfills: if the top job is waiting for, say, 40 nodes to free up, Slurm slots a smaller, shorter job into the gap now, as long as that doesn’t delay the top job’s reserved start time. This is why a 20-minute test can start immediately even when the queue looks deep, and why short jobs start sooner than long ones. Requesting less time and fewer resources makes your job backfill-eligible in more gaps — another payoff for right-sizing.

If sprio shows a low QOS factor because you’re on long but the job would finish in 10 hours, resubmitting under fast is the most effective change you can make.

title: 16  Job arrays
text:
16.1 The problem it solves
You have 500 parameter combinations to sweep, or 500 raster tiles / watersheds / weather-days to process. A bash loop runs them serially in one job, so one crash near the end wastes everything. Copy-pasting 500 submit scripts is no better. An array job is one script, submitted once, that Slurm turns into 500 independent tasks it can run in parallel and backfill wherever there’s room.

title: 16  Job arrays
text:
16.2 The mechanics
Add --array and use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick which piece of work this task does:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro
#SBATCH --job-name=sweep
#SBATCH --array=1-500                 # 500 tasks, indices 1..500
#SBATCH --qos=fast                    # short independent tasks → high-priority QOS
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00               # per task
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=logs/sweep-%A_%a.out # %A = array job id, %a = task index

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 python/3.12.0

# Use the task index to select this task's work:
python run_case.py --case-id ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
Submit once:
mkdir -p logs
sbatch submit_array.sh        # creates 500 tasks: 12345_1, 12345_2, ... 12345_500
Each task is scheduled independently. Because they’re small and short, they backfill well (Chapter 14) and the whole sweep finishes faster than running them in series.

title: 16  Job arrays
text:
16.3 Driving work from the index
The index is just a number; you map it to real work. Common patterns:
Line N of a parameter file:
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" params.txt)
python run.py $PARAM
The Nth input file:
FILES=(/project/cowy-firesurro/data/tiles/*.tif)
THIS=${FILES[$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID]}      # note: arrays are 0-indexed in bash
python process.py "$THIS"
(If you index files from a bash array, start --array=0; if you use sed -n Np, start --array=1. Off-by-one here is the classic array bug.)

title: 16  Job arrays
text:
16.4 Throttling
Cap how many tasks run simultaneously with %:
#SBATCH --array=1-500%20        # at most 20 tasks running at a time
This keeps you under your account’s core cap (and protects your fair-share, Chapter 14) while still processing all 500. A modest % limit is often faster overall, because you stop competing with yourself and stay backfill-friendly.

title: 16  Job arrays
text:
16.5 Managing an array
squeue --me                     # shows pending tasks collapsed, e.g. 12345_[6-500]
scancel 12345                   # cancel the whole array
scancel 12345_7                 # cancel just task 7
sacct -j 12345                  # per-task outcomes after the fact
To find which tasks failed (so you can rerun only those):
sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,State,ExitCode -n | grep -v COMPLETED
then resubmit just those indices: sbatch --array=17,43,88 submit_array.sh.






Arrays vs. MPI jobs



An array is for independent tasks that don’t communicate: sweeps, ensembles, per-file pipelines. If your tasks must talk to each other — a single domain-decomposed simulation — use an MPI job instead (Chapter 20).


Arrays are also the natural unit for ensembles — fire-weather members, hydrologic scenarios, Monte-Carlo draws — one array task per member, each writing to its own output, collected afterward.

text:
17.1 Interactive sessions with salloc
For hands-on work — debugging a crash, exploring a dataset, building a model interactively — request an interactive allocation:
salloc requires at least --account and --time. It grants a shell on a compute node, where you can run heavy work off the login node. The interactive QOS starts in ~10–30 seconds (Chapter 13) with an 8-hour ceiling.

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
text:
18.1 The condo model
Much of MedicineBow’s hardware was purchased by individual research groups. Those inv-* partitions belong to their investors, who get top priority (QOS 110) on them. Everyone else’s jobs can backfill onto idle investor nodes — free capacity most of the time, with one condition.
crumbs: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
text:
An investor can reclaim a node and requeue your job



If you land on investor hardware and the owner submits work, your job is preempted — Slurm kills it and, by default here, requeues it: it returns to the pending queue and starts over from the beginning when resources free up. Any progress not written to disk is lost. This can happen minutes into a job or days in.
crumbs: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
section: 18.2 Two ways to protect a long run
text:
18.2 Two ways to protect a long run
1. Run where you can’t be preempted. Submit long production jobs to the non-preemptible pool:
#SBATCH --partition=non-investor        # 110 CPU nodes, not reclaimable
# or non-investor-gpu for GPU work
This is the right home for anything long that you haven’t checkpointed. (The --constraint=non-investor some docs mention does not work — it’s a partition, not a constraint. See Chapter 12.)
2. Checkpoint, so preemption is cheap. If you run on borrowable hardware (or list several partitions for faster starts), save state periodically so a requeue is survivable.
crumbs: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
text:
18.3 Checkpointing
A checkpoint is a periodic save of enough state to resume rather than restart. It protects against preemption, node failures, and hitting your walltime limit. Any job measured in days should checkpoint.
The pattern:

Every so often (every N iterations, or every ~30–60 min of wall time), write current state to a checkpoint file in /gscratch or /project — not /lscratch, which is wiped when the job ends (Chapter 5).
On startup, check for a checkpoint and resume from it if present, otherwise start fresh.
Write checkpoints atomically (write to a temp file, then rename) so a crash mid-write can’t corrupt your only checkpoint. Keep the last one or two.

Many scientific codes have this built in — WRF has restart files, PyTorch has torch.save/load for model+optimizer state, PETSc and Sundials have checkpoint hooks. Turn these on and set the interval to your risk tolerance.
Auto-resubmit on requeue. Combine checkpointing with a self-resubmitting job so a preempted or timed-out job resumes automatically:
#SBATCH --requeue                          # allow this job to be requeued
#SBATCH --open-mode=append                 # don't clobber the log on requeue
#SBATCH --signal=B:USR1@120                # send USR1 120s before the walltime kill

# resume from checkpoint if one exists
if [ -f state.ckpt ]; then
    ./simulate --restart state.ckpt
else
    ./simulate --fresh
fi
The --signal line asks Slurm to warn your script 120 seconds before the walltime kill; trap that signal to flush a final checkpoint.
crumbs: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing

title: 18  Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing
text:
18.4 Requeue behavior worth knowing

A requeued job keeps its job ID but starts its command from the beginning — Slurm doesn’t magically resume your program; your checkpoint does.
--open-mode=append stops the requeued run from overwriting the previous log.
Check whether a job was requeued with sacct -j <id> --format=JobID,State,Start,End — you’ll see multiple rows.







Checkpoint jobs that run longer than a few hours



Short jobs (minutes to an hour or two) can just be rerun if something goes wrong. Any multi-hour or multi-day job should checkpoint, and any long production run should also prefer non-investor. A non-preemptible partition plus checkpoints is what lets big simulations finish reliably on a shared machine.

title: 19  When jobs fail
text:
19.2 Out of memory
A job that exceeds its memory reservation is killed by the Linux OOM killer — you’ll see OUT_OF_MEMORY in sacct, and often a truncated or empty output file.
sacct -j 123456 --format=JobID,State,MaxRSS,ReqMem
# MaxRSS is peak memory actually used; compare to ReqMem
If MaxRSS is near or above ReqMem, raise --mem and resubmit. Then use seff (Chapter 15) on the successful run to right-size going forward. Note the 10 GB/core default on mb (Chapter 11) — sometimes you already had enough memory and something else was wrong.

title: 19  When jobs fail
text:
19.3 Timeout
TIMEOUT means your job was still running when the clock ran out and Slurm killed it. Options, in order of preference:

Checkpoint so the next run resumes instead of restarting (Section 18.3). This is the durable fix for genuinely long work.
Raise --time — but staying under your QOS ceiling (normal = 3 d, long = 7 d), and knowing a longer request may wait longer to start (Chapter 13).
Make the job finish faster — more cores if it scales, or a smaller problem per job (an array, Chapter 16).

title: 19  When jobs fail
text:
19.4 Your program crashed (FAILED)
FAILED with a non-zero exit code is usually your code, not the cluster. Read the output:
cat slurm-123456.out          # stdout+stderr (or separate --error file)
Common cluster-specific culprits:

Module not loaded in the script. Interactive worked, batch didn’t — because you loaded modules on the login node but not inside the submit script. Put module load in the script (Chapter 10).
Wrong paths. A relative path that existed where you ran sbatch but not where the job ran. Use absolute paths or $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR.
conda env not activated in the script (Chapter 8).
Wrote to /lscratch and it vanished — that’s node-local and wiped at job end (Chapter 5).

title: 19  When jobs fail
text:
19.5 Node failure and preemption
NODE_FAIL (hardware died) and PREEMPTED/REQUEUED (investor reclaimed the node, Chapter 18) are not your bug. The response is the same: checkpoint so a restart is cheap, run long jobs on non-investor, and add --requeue so they come back automatically. If node failures recur on the same node, report it to arcc-help@uwyo.edu with the job ID.

title: 19  When jobs fail
text:
19.6 A debugging loop

sacct -j <id> ... → get the State, narrowing it to one of the four families above.
Resource-related (OOM/timeout) → adjust --mem/--time, resubmit.
FAILED → read slurm-<id>.out, fix the code/env, and reproduce it fast in a debug-QOS job (near-instant start, Chapter 13) rather than waiting in a long queue each iteration.
Once it works, seff <id> → right-size → promote to the real partition/QOS.

Use the debug partition as your fast edit-run-debug loop, and graduate to big queues only once the job is known-good.

title: 20  The parallelism ladder
text:
20.1 Climb only as high as you need
MPI and GPUs sound like “real HPC,” but the right answer is usually lower on the ladder and simpler. Match the rung to the shape of your problem.
flowchart LR
    A["Serial<br/>1 core"] --> B["Job array<br/>many independent runs"]
    B --> C["Multicore<br/>threads, 1 node"]
    C --> D["MPI<br/>1 program, many nodes"]
    D --> E["GPU<br/>ML / PINNs"]
    style B stroke-width:3px,stroke:#4a2c82




Figure 20.1: The parallelism ladder. Climb only as high as the problem needs; most work is solved at the job-array rung (highlighted).

title: 20  The parallelism ladder
text:
20.1.1 Rung 1 — Serial
One core, one task. Fine for small jobs, and the right baseline: get it correct on one core first. If a serial job is fast enough, you’re done — don’t parallelize unnecessarily.
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1


20.1.2 Rung 2 — Job array (many independent serial runs)
If you need to run the same thing many times over different inputs — a parameter sweep, an ensemble, per-file processing — this is almost always the answer. Low complexity, and it backfills well (Chapter 16).
#SBATCH --array=1-500%20
python run.py --id ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
Use this whenever “I need to run it N times” applies.


20.1.3 Rung 3 — Multicore (one program, many threads, one node)
If a single run is too slow and your code is multithreaded (OpenMP, or numpy/xarray/PyTorch using many cores), give it more cores on one node:
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
./my_threaded_program
Only ask for as many cores as your code actually scales to — check with seff afterward (Chapter 11). Doubling cores rarely doubles speed.


20.1.4 Rung 4 — MPI (one program across many nodes)
When a single problem is too big for one node — a domain-decomposed simulation like WRF, where pieces must exchange data every step — you need MPI: one program, many processes across many nodes, communicating.
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks=384                 # e.g. 96 tasks/node × 4 nodes
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 openmpi/5.0.10
srun ./my_mpi_simulation             # srun launches the MPI ranks
Use srun (not mpirun) to launch — it’s integrated with Slurm and gets the task layout right automatically. MPI is a step up in complexity; use it only when a problem won’t fit on one node. For long MPI runs, prefer non-investor and checkpoint (Chapter 18).


20.1.5 Rung 5 — GPU
For workloads built for GPUs — deep learning, PINNs, some CFD/linear algebra — a GPU can beat dozens of CPU cores, but only if your code actually targets the GPU (Section 17.2); a CPU program gains nothing from a GPU node except a longer queue. Develop on mb-a30, scale up to mb-h100 for real training (Chapter 13).
#SBATCH --partition=mb-a30
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
module load gcc/13.2.0 cuda-toolkit/12.6.1
python train.py

21.10 Common mistakes to avoid

--account=<project> is required on every job.
On mb, no --mem → 10 GB per core silently. Always set --mem.
Nothing is backed up. Keep a copy off-cluster.
Install software in /project/<proj>/software, not /home (50 GB).
module spider, not module avail.
Long jobs → non-investor partition and checkpoint (investors preempt).
Never compute on the login node. Use sbatch/salloc.
Use tmux so a dropped connection doesn’t kill interactive work.

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.1 Login and access
A symptom-first index to the rest of the book.
“Permission denied (publickey)” when I ssh — it worked before. Your SSH key almost certainly expired (they last one year). Regenerate it in the portal’s SSH Key Manager, unzip into ~/.ssh, chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh (Chapter 3).
“Permission denied” on a brand-new setup. Check permissions: chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh, and make sure you unzipped the key into ~/.ssh. Confirm you’re using medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu, not the dead southpass name.
I can’t get an account at all. Only a PI can request it, in writing, against a project. You cannot self-register (Chapter 2).
Globus won’t let me add the collection. If you’re an external collaborator on an ARCC-Only account, you can’t use Globus. You need a UW-side guest collection (Chapter 6).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.2 Jobs won’t submit
sbatch: error: ... You have to specify an account. Add --account=cowy-firesurro (Chapter 10).
Job violates accounting/QOS policy (...) at submit time. Your request exceeds a QOS limit (every QOS is DenyOnLimit). Usually --time exceeds the QOS ceiling — e.g. 5 days under normal (max 3 d). Lower --time or switch QOS (Chapter 12). Check ceilings with sqos and showuserlimits.
Invalid qos specification. Your account can’t use that QOS. Yours are debug, fast, interactive, long, normal (sacctmgr -n show assoc user=$USER format=qos).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.3 Jobs won’t start
Stuck in PENDING with reason Priority. The machine is just busy and you’re in line. Either wait, or pick a higher-priority (shorter) QOS — QOS dominates priority here (Chapter 14). Small/short jobs backfill sooner.
Stuck with reason Resources. You asked for a lot (many cores, much memory, a scarce GPU). Right-size (Chapter 11), or accept the wait. showjobreasons <id> explains in plain language.
GPU job pending for hours. H100/L40S are heavily contended (Chapter 13). Develop on mb-a30 instead, and check gpuavail/showpartitions for what’s actually free before submitting.
Pending with QOSMax... or AssocGrpCpuLimit. You (or your account) hit a cap — e.g. too many cores in flight at once. Wait for your other jobs to finish, or throttle an array with % (Chapter 16).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.4 Jobs fail
OUT_OF_MEMORY. Raise --mem. Compare MaxRSS to ReqMem in sacct (Chapter 19). Watch the 10 GB/core default trap (Chapter 11).
TIMEOUT. Job outran --time. Checkpoint (Section 18.3), raise --time within the QOS ceiling, or split the work into an array.
FAILED, worked interactively but not in batch. You loaded modules / activated conda on the login node but not inside the submit script. Put them in the script (Chapter 10, Chapter 8).
Output file references files that “don’t exist.” Relative paths from the wrong directory, or you wrote to /lscratch (wiped at job end). Use absolute paths or $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR; copy /lscratch output out before the job ends (Chapter 5).
PREEMPTED / REQUEUED on a long job. You were on investor hardware and got reclaimed. Move to --partition=non-investor and checkpoint (Chapter 18).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.5 Software
“That module doesn’t exist” but I’m sure it does. module avail only shows what’s reachable now. Use module spider <name> — you probably need to load a compiler first (Chapter 7).
CUDA won’t build / link. Load gcc/13.2.0 (not 14) — cuda-toolkit is built against 13.2 despite its deprecation warning (Chapter 7).
Home directory full, everything breaking. Conda in /home. Move envs to /project/<proj>/software via ~/.condarc, and clean up (Chapter 8). Check with du -sh ~/* | sort -h.
GPU job runs but is slow / nvidia-smi shows 0%. Your code isn’t actually on the GPU. Verify the framework sees CUDA; in a container, you need --nv (Section 17.2).

title: 22  Troubleshooting
text:
22.6 Still stuck?
Email arcc-help@uwyo.edu with your job ID, the submit script, and the error. Or bring it to office hours, Tuesdays 11am–1pm on Zoom. Include what you already tried — it gets you a faster answer.

title: 23  Glossary
text:
Plain-language definitions of the terms this book uses.

Account (Slurm)

The project that a job is charged to (e.g. cowy-firesurro). Required on every job via --account. Not your username. See Chapter 10.

ARCC

Advanced Research Computing Center — the UW group that runs MedicineBow.

ASCEND / ARID

The NSF Regional Innovation Engine (ASCEND) and its wildfire-resilience program (ARID) that many readers of this book work under. See the preface.

Backfill

Slurm slotting a small, short job into a gap in the schedule without delaying higher-priority jobs. Why short jobs start fast. See Chapter 14.

Batch job

A job submitted as a script with sbatch that runs unattended when scheduled. The normal way to run work. See Chapter 10.

Checkpoint

A periodic save of a job’s state so it can resume instead of restart after a preemption, timeout, or crash. Essential for long jobs. See Section 18.3.

Compute node

A machine where computation actually runs, allocated to you by Slurm. Distinct from a login node. See Chapter 1.

Condo model

The funding model where research groups buy nodes (inv-*) and others borrow them when idle, subject to reclaim/preemption. See Chapter 18.

Core-hour

One CPU core used for one hour — the unit your allocation is measured in. Reserving 8 cores for 1 hour costs 8 core-hours whether or not you use them.

DenyOnLimit

A QOS flag meaning an over-limit request is rejected at submit time, not silently queued. See Chapter 12.

Fair-share

A priority factor reflecting your account’s recent usage relative to its share; heavy recent use temporarily lowers your priority. See Chapter 14.

GRES (Generic RESource)

How you request GPUs: --gres=gpu:1 or --gres=gpu:h100:2. See Section 17.2.

Investor / inv-*

Nodes/partitions owned by a specific group, who get top priority; others can be preempted off them. See Chapter 18.

Job array

One script run many times with a varying index ($SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID), for parameter sweeps and ensembles. Max 10,000 tasks. See Chapter 16.

Lmod / module

The system that loads specific software versions into your shell on demand. Hierarchical: many modules are hidden until you load a compiler. Use module spider. See Chapter 7.

Login node

The shared front-end machine (mblog1, mblog2) you land on when you connect. For editing and submitting — not for computing. See Chapter 1.

MedicineBow

UW/ARCC’s current flagship HPC cluster. The subject of this book.

MPI

Message Passing Interface — the standard for a single parallel program spanning many cores or nodes that communicate. Launched with srun. Contrast with job arrays. See Chapter 20.

OnDemand (Open OnDemand)

The web portal at medicinebow.arcc.uwyo.edu — file browser, terminal, and interactive apps. See Chapter 3.

OOM (Out Of Memory)

When a job exceeds its memory reservation and is killed. Fix by raising --mem. See Chapter 19.

Partition

A named pool of nodes with particular hardware (mb, mb-h100, teton, non-investor, …). Chosen with --partition. See Chapter 12.

Preemption

An investor reclaiming a borrowed node, causing your job to be killed and (here) requeued. See Chapter 18.

Priority

The score that orders pending jobs. On MedicineBow it’s dominated by QOS (weight 200). See Chapter 14.

QOS (Quality of Service)

The service tier that sets your max walltime, resource cap, and priority (debug, fast, normal, long, …). See Chapter 12.

Requeue

Putting a killed (preempted/failed) job back in the pending queue to start over. Pair with checkpointing. See Chapter 18.

Scratch (/gscratch, $SCRATCH)

Fast, large, temporary storage purged after 90 days of inactivity. Not backed up. See Chapter 5.

seff

A command showing a finished job’s CPU and memory efficiency — use it to right-size. See Chapter 15.

Slurm

The scheduler that manages all jobs on the cluster. See Chapter 9.

Snapshot

A point-in-time copy of a filesystem, on the same array as the live data. Protects against accidental deletion, not hardware loss. Not a backup. See Chapter 5.

Walltime

Real elapsed clock time a job is allowed (--time). The job is killed at the limit. See Chapter 11.
